question: What is the primary purpose of using barium sulfate during a barium meal examination?

options.B: To act as a radiopaque contrast medium that outlines the upper GI tract
options.C: To sedate the patient during fluoroscopy
options.D: To stimulate rapid intestinal motility and peristalsis

explanation: Barium sulfate is a radiopaque contrast agent that coats the mucosal lining of the upper GI tract, making internal structures clearly visible on X-rays. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T14#GNS221_U2_T14_h1)

question: Which of the following anatomical structures are specifically evaluated during a barium meal procedure?
explanation: A barium meal is specifically designed to examine the upper GI tract, encompassing the pharynx, esophagus, stomach, and duodenum. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T14#GNS221_U2_T14_h1)

question: Which of the following clinical symptoms is a primary indication for scheduling a barium meal examination?

options.A: Lower right quadrant pain associated with appendicitis

explanation: Dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) and persistent dyspepsia are key indications for evaluating the upper GI tract using a barium meal. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T14#GNS221_U2_T14_h2)

question: Why is the barium meal examination particularly valuable in certain healthcare settings, such as some facilities in Nigeria?

options.A: It completely replaces the need for any blood tests.
options.B: It is a reliable, cost-effective diagnostic tool when advanced endoscopy is unavailable.
options.C: It is the only imaging test that uses ionizing radiation.
options.D: It requires no patient cooperation or preparation.

explanation: A barium meal serves as a cost-effective and reliable alternative for visualizing upper GI abnormalities where specialized endoscopic equipment may be scarce. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T14#GNS221_U2_T14_h2)

question: What is the absolute contraindication for performing a standard barium meal examination?
explanation: Suspected or known GI perforation is an absolute contraindication because leaked barium causes severe peritonitis or mediastinitis. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T14#GNS221_U2_T14_h3)

question: What type of contrast medium is typically substituted if a patient has a suspected bowel perforation?
explanation: Water-soluble contrast agents are used instead of barium when perforation is suspected because they are safely absorbed by the body if they leak into tissues. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T14#GNS221_U2_T14_h3)

question: Why must a patient remain NPO (nil per os) for 6 to 8 hours before a barium meal?

options.A: To prevent sudden drops in systemic blood pressure
options.B: To ensure the stomach is empty so food does not obscure internal lesions
options.C: To stimulate the rapid production of gastric acid
options.D: To allow the kidneys to concentrate urine

explanation: An empty stomach is necessary because leftover food or fluid can obscure ulcers, polyps, or tumors, leading to inaccurate diagnostic results. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T14#GNS221_U2_T14_h4)

question: What instruction should a nurse give to a patient who smokes regarding the morning of the barium meal?

options.A: Smoke as normal to keep the patient calm.
options.B: Smoke only immediately after drinking the barium suspension.
options.C: Refrain from smoking because nicotine stimulates gastric secretions and motility.
options.D: Double the usual cigarette intake to dilate the esophagus.

explanation: Smoking stimulates gastric acid secretion and motility, which can alter the appearance of the stomach and interfere with accurate radiologic imaging. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T14#GNS221_U2_T14_h4)

question: What is the purpose of swallowing gas-producing crystals during a double-contrast barium meal?

options.A: To neutralize stomach acid and relieve heartburn
options.B: To produce carbon dioxide that distends the stomach and highlights mucosal details
options.C: To accelerate the elimination of barium from the bowel
options.D: To sedate the patient and reduce anxiety

explanation: Gas-producing crystals release carbon dioxide to inflate the stomach, allowing the radiologist to clearly view fine mucosal details in a double-contrast study. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T14#GNS221_U2_T14_h5)

question: Why is the patient asked to assume various positions (such as supine, prone, and oblique) during the fluoroscopy?

options.A: To ensure the barium suspension uniformly coats the entire mucosal lining
options.B: To speed up the clearance of barium into the large intestine
options.C: To prevent the patient from falling asleep on the table
options.D: To measure the patient's range of motion and joint flexibility

explanation: Changing positions allows gravity to help the barium suspension thoroughly and evenly coat all areas of the upper GI tract mucosa. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T14#GNS221_U2_T14_h5)

question: What is a primary reason for encouraging high fluid intake following a barium meal examination?

options.A: To dilute stomach acid and prevent ulcers
options.B: To prevent barium hardening and subsequent fecal impaction
options.C: To accelerate the absorption of barium into the bloodstream
options.D: To prevent immediate post-procedure nausea and vomiting

explanation: Barium absorbs water in the intestines and can harden, so drinking plenty of fluids is essential to prevent fecal impaction and constipation. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T14#GNS221_U2_T14_h6)

question: What should the nurse tell the patient to expect regarding their bowel movements over the next 24 to 72 hours?

options.A: Stools will turn bright red or black due to blood loss.
options.B: Stools will appear chalky, pale, or whitish-gray.
options.C: Bowel movements will cease completely for a week.
options.D: Stools will have an extremely foul, sulfur-like odor.

explanation: The elimination of residual barium causes stools to look chalky, pale, or whitish-gray, which is a normal finding that should be explained to the patient. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T14#GNS221_U2_T14_h6)

question: What is the most common minor complication experienced by patients following a barium meal?
explanation: Constipation is the most common complication because barium absorbs intestinal water and hardens as it passes through the colon. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T14#GNS221_U2_T14_h7)

question: What complication should the nurse monitor for if a patient with severe dysphagia undergoes a barium meal?
explanation: Patients with impaired swallowing are at high risk of aspirating barium into the respiratory tract, leading to chemical pneumonitis and respiratory distress. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T14#GNS221_U2_T14_h7)
